subject: Tokenizer boundary artifacts and their propagation through downstream task-specific fine-tuning objectives
prompt:
Topic: Tokenizer boundary artifacts and their propagation through downstream task-specific fine-tuning objectives

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-3332)
response:
Tokenization splits text into subword units before any learning happens, meaning the model never sees raw characters — it sees a vocabulary of ~30K–100K tokens whose boundaries were fixed by an algorithm (BPE, WordPiece, Unigram) trained on a generic corpus. The central question is: when those boundaries systematically misalign with the linguistic or task-relevant units that matter (morpheme boundaries, named entity spans, code identifiers, numerical digits), does fine-tuning on a downstream objective merely work around the artifact, or does it encode the artifact into the task-specific weights in ways that compound? A beginner assumes fine-tuning is a corrective — that gradient updates on task data will teach the model to ignore bad splits. The expert worries about the opposite: that the fine-tuning loss surface is shaped by tokenization from the start, so a token like "un##able" versus "una##ble" isn't just an aesthetic difference — it changes which embedding dimensions carry morphological signal, which attention heads fire across spans, and which gradient paths are reinforced. The deeper concern is distributional: artifacts aren't uniformly distributed across the vocabulary, so rare tokens, code-mixed text, and numerals accumulate disproportionate boundary noise, and a fine-tuning objective with no explicit character-level supervision has no mechanism to correct this — it optimizes what it can see, and it can only see the token sequence it was handed.

In BIO tagging, each token receives exactly one label, so when a tokenizer like BPE splits "Schwarzenegger" into ["Sch", "war", "zen", "egg", "er"], the canonical annotation assigns B-PER to the first subword and I-PER to the rest — but this is a convention, not a linguistic fact, and different frameworks (IOB2, IOBES, label-the-first-only) make different choices, producing incompatible training signals for the same underlying entity. The loss gradient during fine-tuning treats each subword prediction as an independent cross-entropy term, so a 5-subword entity contributes 5 gradient updates, artificially upweighting entities that tokenize into many pieces and downweighting compact ones — a systematic bias that has nothing to do with entity salience or frequency. Empirically, Rust et al. (2021) "How Good is Your Tokenizer?" showed that NER performance on multilingual benchmarks dropped substantially for languages where the mBERT tokenizer was trained on little data, producing high token-to-word ratios and frequent unknown-subword splits; the degradation was not uniform but concentrated on entity types with morphologically complex surface forms. The gradient distortion compounds during fine-tuning because the I-PER predictions on interior subwords receive signal only about continuation, never about entity onset — meaning the B/I distinction, which carries the boundary detection load, is learned from a small fraction of the subword sequence and is disproportionately influenced by whatever the first subword of a rare entity happens to look like. What experts track but beginners miss is that this isn't just a labeling inconvenience: the model's span-boundary representations are being shaped by tokenizer accidents, so at inference time, entities whose surface form tokenizes differently from their training instances (due to casing, hyphenation, or code-mixing) fail not because the model lacks world knowledge but because the gradient signal for boundary detection was never aligned to character-level or morphological reality.

When you swap the tokenizer, the new vocabulary contains tokens — say, "Schwarzenegger" as a single unit — that have no corresponding row in the pretrained embedding matrix, so those rows must be initialized somehow while the transformer body (attention weights, FFN, LayerNorm parameters) remains frozen and was trained to expect inputs in the geometry of the old embedding space. The standard fallback is to initialize new token embeddings by averaging the old subword embeddings that compose them: "Schwarzenegger" → mean(["Sch", "war", "zen", "egg", "er"]), but this is geometrically wrong because the old embeddings were never trained as compositional primitives — they were trained as contextual anchors whose meaning is completed by attention over neighboring tokens, so their average does not occupy the region of embedding space the frozen transformer expects for a single-token named entity. Minixhofer et al. (2022) in "WECHSEL" showed this concretely: naive averaging produces embeddings that fall in low-density regions of the pretrained space, causing the frozen attention layers to produce anomalous attention distributions because the query-key dot products assume a particular norm and angular distribution that averaged embeddings violate. The problem is further compounded by positional encoding: the pretrained model learned that a 5-token span of subwords carries positional variation across those 5 positions, but a single merged token collapses that span to one position, so the frozen positional-plus-token embedding sum lands nowhere the model was trained to process. You could unfreeze the embedding layer and fine-tune only it, but then you're in a different trap: the embedding layer's gradients depend on the frozen transformer's backward pass, which was calibrated to a different token distribution, so the learning signal for new tokens is noisy and slow to converge — Sachidananda et al. (2023) estimated that token embedding convergence requires roughly 10× more updates than task head convergence when the token distribution shifts substantially. The core reason interpolation fails isn't a lack of cleverness in the averaging scheme; it's that pretrained token embeddings encode positional role in a specific segmentation regime, not decomposable semantic content, and no static combination of old embeddings can reconstruct the role a new token needs to play in a system whose weights were frozen to expect the old regime.

The fusion mechanism — typically a learned weighted sum, a small MLP, or a cross-attention layer projecting character representations into subword space — is trained end-to-end with the task loss, which means its gradients flow only through whatever character-level variation covaries with task-relevant distinctions in the fine-tuning data. For NER, that means the character encoder gets gradient signal when character features help distinguish entity vs. non-entity tokens, but receives no signal for boundary artifacts that happen to be consistent across the fine-tuning set — if "Schwarzenegger" always appears intact in training, the fusion layer learns nothing about how to handle its fragmented tokenization because the artifact never creates a loss-visible error. This is the core problem documented in the CANINE paper (Clark et al., 2022): character-level representations are rich, but without supervision that explicitly rewards boundary-sensitive behavior, the fusion gate tends to collapse toward weighting the subword embedding heavily and the character embedding weakly, because the subword embedding is already a strong prior and the gradient penalty for ignoring character features is small when task accuracy is high. The result is a fusion mechanism that behaves like a residual correction rather than a genuine character-level grounding — the character encoder survives in the architecture but contributes primarily to surface-form disambiguation (capitalization, punctuation) rather than to morphological boundary recovery, which is exactly the failure mode you wanted to fix. Empirically, Aguilar et al. (2021) showed in a code-switching NER setting that hybrid character-subword models only outperformed pure subword baselines when the fine-tuning data contained sufficient within-entity surface variation — when it didn't, the character pathway was effectively dormant at inference despite being present in the model. The expert worry here is a kind of gradient laziness: the task loss is indifferent to why a prediction is correct, so the optimizer finds the shortest path to low loss, which is almost always to trust the pretrained subword representations and treat the character encoder as a tie-breaker, leaving the tokenization artifact unaddressed in exactly the cases — rare entities, unseen morphological variants — where you needed it most.

The alignment or interference is determined primarily by the cosine similarity between the task gradient vector and the auxiliary gradient vector in the shared fusion layer's parameter space — when they point in similar directions, the auxiliary loss accelerates convergence on features the task loss would have found anyway; when they conflict, the optimizer is pulled toward a compromise that may be suboptimal for both. The conflict is most likely when the masked character prediction objective rewards memorizing surface statistics (common letter n-grams, capitalization patterns) while the task loss rewards span-level semantic distinctions, because these objectives make competing demands on the same fusion weights: character prediction wants the fusion layer to preserve high-frequency orthographic features, while NER wants it to suppress them in favor of contextual entity signals. Yuqing Tang et al. and the broader multi-task learning literature (including Standley et al., 2020, "Which Tasks Should Be Learned Together?") establish that task gradient conflict scales with the degree to which the tasks require different feature selectivity from shared layers — and character prediction and token-level classification differ in exactly this way, since one is local and position-sensitive while the other is contextual and span-sensitive. The loss weighting hyperparameter λ between the two objectives is not a simple knob: because the character loss operates at finer granularity (one gradient update per masked character vs. one per token), it contributes more frequent but lower-magnitude gradient steps, meaning even a small λ can dominate the fusion layer update frequency and effectively overwrite task-relevant curvature in the loss landscape. Gradient surgery (Yu et al., 2020) offers a principled fix — project the auxiliary gradient onto the orthogonal complement of the task gradient whenever they conflict — but this requires computing per-layer gradient cosine similarities at each step, which is computationally expensive and rarely done in practice for fine-tuning regimes. The deeper structural issue is that the fusion layer occupies a bottleneck position where both losses converge, making it the most contested parameter group in the network; empirically, Aghajanyan et al. (2021) showed that auxiliary objectives during fine-tuning reduce the effective intrinsic dimensionality of the task loss landscape only when the auxiliary gradient consistently reinforces low-rank structure already present in the task gradient — otherwise they increase dimensionality and slow convergence.

Moving the auxiliary character loss to an earlier, architecturally isolated layer — say, supervising only the character encoder's own output projection before it feeds the fusion layer — does reduce direct gradient conflict in the fusion weights, but it relocates the problem to the interface between the character encoder's output distribution and the fusion layer's input expectations. The character encoder, now trained by its own loss, will converge to represent features that minimize masked character prediction error, which means it develops an output distribution shaped by orthographic statistics rather than by what the fusion layer needs to produce task-useful subword augmentations — the two modules optimize toward different attractors and the fusion layer must bridge an increasingly mismatched representation gap. This is a specific instance of the broader "gradient isolation fallacy" in modular networks: isolating gradients prevents interference in shared weights but does not prevent representational divergence, where upstream modules drift into feature spaces that are locally optimal for their own loss but progressively less useful as inputs to downstream components. Pfeiffer et al. (2021) in the adapter fusion literature observed exactly this: when adapter modules are trained with objectives that don't share gradient paths with the main model, the adapted representations become harder for the frozen transformer layers to interpret, requiring additional projection capacity to realign them — adding parameters to solve a problem that architectural isolation was supposed to eliminate. The only clean resolution is to ensure the auxiliary loss either shares enough of the computational graph with the task loss that their gradients are naturally coupled, or to accept that isolation requires an explicit alignment mechanism — a learned projection, a contrastive objective between character and subword representations, or periodic joint fine-tuning passes — that reintroduces the interference you were trying to avoid. In practice, the empirical result from CharBERT (Ma et al., 2020) is instructive: their character-subword interaction module worked best when the character loss was not isolated but instead allowed to propagate through the shared interaction layer, accepting some gradient conflict as the price of keeping the two representation spaces mutually legible.

The minimum conditions reduce to three geometric requirements that can be stated task-agnostically: the character encoder's output manifold and the subword transformer's input manifold must overlap sufficiently that interpolations between them remain in-distribution for the fusion layer; the two encoders must share at least one class of invariance (e.g., both must be insensitive to the same set of surface perturbations, or both must preserve the same notion of token identity under morphological variation); and the mutual information between character representations and subword representations must remain above a threshold that prevents either from becoming a near-constant function of the other's input. The first condition fails when isolated training drives the character encoder toward a high-entropy orthographic space while the subword transformer occupies a low-entropy contextual space — the manifolds separate, and the fusion layer is asked to bridge a gap that grows with each gradient step that doesn't couple them. The second condition is the most theoretically precise: Wang & Isola (2020) in "Understanding Contrastive Representation Learning" showed that alignment between two encoders requires that they assign similar representations to inputs that should be treated as equivalent — without a shared equivalence class, there is no stable attractor for joint training, and the two modules will find different solutions to the same surface variation. The third condition rules out a degenerate solution that technically satisfies the first two: a character encoder that collapses all representations to a single point is trivially aligned with anything but contributes zero information, which is the "gradient laziness" failure mode we identified earlier now expressed as an information-theoretic collapse. Tito Johansson et al. and the BYOL/VICReg literature (Bardes et al., 2022) established that preventing this collapse requires either negative samples, variance regularization, or an asymmetric architecture that breaks the symmetry between the two encoders — all of which are mechanisms for enforcing a lower bound on the entropy of each encoder's output distribution independently of task loss. The implication for tokenizer artifact correction is pointed: no purely task-supervised objective can guarantee these three conditions are met, because task supervision is indifferent to the internal geometry of the character encoder as long as the task loss is minimized — satisfying all three conditions requires an objective that explicitly measures the relationship between the two representation spaces, which is precisely what contrastive or variance-regularized pre-training provides and what fine-tuning alone cannot.

Tokenizer boundary artifacts are fundamentally a pre-training problem in the sense that the embedding geometry — the spatial relationships between token representations that all downstream fine-tuning inherits — is fixed during pre-training, and no fine-tuning objective can restructure that geometry without either catastrophic forgetting or the auxiliary loss machinery we've shown to be insufficient. A pre-training objective explicitly designed for BPE robustness would need to enforce that the representation of a token sequence produced by one valid segmentation of a string is close in embedding space to the representation produced by an alternative segmentation of the same string — call this a segmentation invariance objective, analogous to how data augmentation in vision enforces that rotated and cropped views of the same image map to nearby representations. Concretely, this means during pre-training, for each training string you sample two tokenizations — the standard BPE segmentation and an alternative produced by dropout, subword regularization (Kudo, 2018), or a character-level resegmentation — and apply a contrastive or consistency loss that penalizes large distances between the two sequence representations in the transformer's hidden space. Kudo's subword regularization (used in SentencePiece) already does this implicitly at the tokenizer level by sampling from a unigram language model distribution over segmentations, and Provilkov et al. (2020) extended this with BPE-Dropout, showing that stochastic segmentation during pre-training improved downstream robustness on morphologically rich languages by 1-3 BLEU points — but neither paper applied an explicit representation-level consistency loss, only input-level stochasticity, leaving the model to discover segmentation invariance through the MLM objective alone. The stronger version would add a representation-level term: after encoding both segmentations through the transformer, require that their [CLS] representations (or mean-pooled sequences) satisfy a VICReg-style variance-covariance constraint, ensuring the model builds a shared semantic space that is genuinely invariant to BPE accidents rather than merely tolerant of them through statistical averaging. The limit of this approach is that segmentation invariance is not always correct — "un-happy" and "unha-ppy" should map to nearby representations, but "the-rapist" and "ther-apist" should not, because the segmentation boundary in the second case is semantically load-bearing — meaning the pre-training objective needs a mechanism to distinguish artifact boundaries from meaningful ones, which requires either linguistic supervision or a learned boundary salience model that is itself vulnerable to the same tokenization problems.
